title: Money talks in Major League Baseball
text:
Money talks in Major League Baseball. Some teams spend hundreds of millions of dollars building their rosters, while others try to compete with a fraction of that amount
In 2026, the Los Angeles Dodgers, New York Mets and New York Yankees had baseball’s three highest payrolls. Meanwhile, the Miami Marlins, Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays had the three lowest.
But does spending more money actually lead to winning more games in the MLB?
Using MLB payroll and team records from 1995 to 2026, the numbers tell an interesting story


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
library(scales)

mlb <- read.csv("mlb_payroll_wins_1995_2026.csv")

mlb <- mlb |>
  mutate(
    team_year = paste(year, team)
  )

highball <- mlb |>
  arrange(desc(payroll)) |>
  head(2) 

lowball <- mlb |>
  filter(payroll < 1e+08, win_pct > .65)

losers <- mlb |>
  filter(payroll > 1.5e+08, win_pct < .400)

ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data=mlb,
    aes(
      x=payroll,
      y=win_pct
    ),
    color="lightgrey"
  ) +
  geom_point(
  data=highball,
  aes(
    x=payroll,
    y=win_pct
  ),
  color="red"
) +
geom_point(
  data=lowball,
  aes(
    x=payroll,
    y=win_pct
  ),
  color="green"
) +
  geom_point(
  data=losers,
  aes(
    x=payroll,
    y=win_pct
  ),
  color="blue"
) +
geom_text_repel(
  data=highball,
  aes(
    x=payroll,
    y=win_pct,
    label=team_year
  )
) +
geom_text_repel(
  data=lowball,
  aes(
    x=payroll,
    y=win_pct,
    label=team_year
  )
) +
geom_text_repel(
  data=losers,
  aes(
    x=payroll,
    y=win_pct,
    label=team_year
  )
) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels=comma)+
labs(
  title= "Big payrolls don't always translate to big wins in MLB",
  subtitle= "From 1995 to 2026, some MLB teams won big with smaller payrolls, while others struggled despite spending millions.",
  caption= "Source: The Baseball Cube | By Keegan Timmins",
  x="Team payroll",
  y="Winning percentage"
) +
theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 19, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=9.8), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
    ) 









Looking at more than three decades of MLB data, there’s no guarantee that spending more money will produce more wins.
The green dots highlight teams that spent less than $100 million but won more than 65% of their games. The blue dots represent teams that spent more than $150 million and finished with losing over 60% of their games. The final color, red represents teams that spent over $350 million dollars that year regardless of success.
WHiles expensive rosters can help teams compete, several smaller budget teams have proven that success doesn’t always require a massive payroll.
But have the same teams always dominated baseball’s spending?


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
library(ggbump)

mlb <- read.csv("mlb_payroll_wins_1995_2026.csv")

rankings <- mlb |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(payroll_rank=rank(-payroll))

high2026 <- mlb |>
  filter(year == 2026) |>
  arrange(desc(payroll)) |>
  head(3)

low2026 <- mlb |>
  filter(year == 2026) |>
  arrange(payroll) |>
  head(3)

highteams <- rankings |>
  filter(team %in% high2026$team)

lowteams <- rankings |>
  filter(team %in% low2026$team)

lowteams <- rankings |>
  filter(team %in% low2026$team |
         team == "Cleveland Indians" | 
         team == "Tampa Bay Devil Rays" |
         team == "Florida Marlins")

lowteams <- lowteams |>
  mutate(
    team=gsub("Cleveland Indians", "Cleveland Guardians", team)
  )

lowteams <- lowteams |>
  mutate(
    team=gsub("Tampa Bay Devil Rays", "Tampa Bay Rays", team)
  )

lowteams <- lowteams |>
  mutate(
    team=gsub("Florida Marlins", "Miami Marlins", team)
  )

cleveland <- lowteams |>
  filter(team == "Cleveland Guardians", year == 2026)

tampa <- lowteams |>
  filter(team == "Tampa Bay Rays", year == 2026)

miami <- lowteams |>
  filter(team == "Miami Marlins", year == 2026)

dodgers <- highteams |>
  filter(team == "Los Angeles Dodgers", year == 2026)

mets <- highteams |>
  filter(team == "New York Mets", year == 2026)

yankees <- highteams |>
  filter(team == "New York Yankees", year == 2026)

ggplot() +
  geom_bump(
    data=rankings,
    aes(
      x=year,
      y=payroll_rank,
      group=team
    ),
    color="lightgrey"
  ) +
  geom_bump(
  data=highteams,
  aes(
    x=year,
    y=payroll_rank,
    group=team
  ),
  color="green"
) +
geom_bump(
  data=lowteams,
  aes(
    x=year,
    y=payroll_rank,
    group=team
  ),
  color="red"
) +
geom_point(
  data=highteams,
  aes(
    x=year,
    y=payroll_rank
  ),
  color="green",
  size=2
) +
geom_point(
  data=lowteams,
  aes(
    x=year,
    y=payroll_rank
  ),
  color="red",
  size=2
) +
  geom_text(
  data=cleveland,
  aes(
    x=year + 5,
    y=payroll_rank -0.5 ,
    label=team
  )
) +
geom_text(
  data=tampa,
  aes(
    x=year + 4.20,
    y=payroll_rank -1.5,
    label=team
  )
) +
  geom_text(
  data=miami,
  aes(
    x=year + 3.5,
    y=payroll_rank +0.5,
    label=team
  )
) +
geom_text(
  data=dodgers,
  aes(
    x=year + 5,
    y=payroll_rank - 1.3,
    label=team
  )
) +
geom_text(
  data=mets,
  aes(
    x=year + 4,
    y=payroll_rank,
    label=team
  )
) +
geom_text(
  data=yankees,
  aes(
    x=year + 4.5,
    y=payroll_rank + 1.3,
    label=team
  )
) +
scale_y_reverse() +
scale_x_continuous(
  breaks=c(1995, 1998, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2026),
  limits=c(1995, 2034)
) +
  labs(
  title= "MLB's highest and lowest payrolls take different paths",
  subtitle="Green shows the three highest-paid MLB teams, while red tracks the three lowest-paid teams from 1995 to 2026.",
  caption= "Source: The Baseball Cube | By Keegan Timmins",
  x="Year",
  y="Team payroll rank"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
  axis.title = element_text(size = 8),
  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
  panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
  plot.title.position = "plot"
)









The second chart tracks the three highest and lowest paid teams from 2026, following them throughout since the 1995 season.
The Dodgers, Mets and Yankees are highlighted in green, while the Marlins, Guardians and Rays are shown in red.
The Yankees have regularly ranked among baseball’s biggest spenders, while the other 2 franchises have experienced changes in their payroll rankings.
But despite their different spending approaches all of these six teams have the same goal. Get to the postseason and win the championship.
So how did these different teams perform in the 2026 season?


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)

mlb <- read.csv("mlb_payroll_wins_1995_2026.csv")

teams2026 <- mlb |>
  filter(year == 2026) |>
  arrange(desc(payroll))

playoffteams <- teams2026 |>
  filter(team %in% c(
    "Tampa Bay Rays",
    "Cleveland Guardians",
    "Houston Astros",
    "New York Yankees",
    "Boston Red Sox",
    "Chicago White Sox",
    "Milwaukee Brewers",
    "Los Angeles Dodgers",
    "Atlanta Braves",
    "San Diego Padres",
    "Chicago Cubs",
    "Philadelphia Phillies"
  ))

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data=teams2026,
    aes(
      y=reorder(team, payroll),
      yend=team,
      x=wins,
      xend=losses
    ),
    color="grey",
    linewidth=1.5
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data=playoffteams,
    aes(
      y=reorder(team, payroll),
      yend=team,
      x=wins,
      xend=losses
    ),
    color="blue",
    linewidth=1.5
  ) +
geom_point(
  data=teams2026,
  aes(
    y=team,
    x=wins
  ),
  color="green",
  size=3
) +
geom_point(
  data=teams2026,
  aes(
    y=team,
    x=losses
  ),
  color="red",
  size=3
) +
labs(
  title="MLB playoff teams succeeded at every payroll level",
  subtitle="The 2026 playoff teams are highlighted in blue, with green showing wins and red showing losses.",
  caption= "Source: The Baseball Cube | By Keegan Timmins",
  x="Number of games",
  y="MLB teams"
) +
theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 8), 
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size=10), 
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title.position = "plot"
    ) 









The final chart compares every team’s win and loss record during the 2026 season, with the playoff teams being highlighted in blue.
Cleveland provides one of the best examples.
Despite having the second lowest payroll in the league, the Guardians finished with a 85-77 record, winning the American League Central and reaching the playoffs.
You take a look at the second most expensive team ever, the 2026 Mets, who finished with a losing record of 74-88, missing the postseason.
Milwaukee also proved that spending the most money isn’t needed to win the most. The Brewers finished 20th in the payroll ranks but finished with the best record at 103-59. This also shows when they won the world series
The data shows that spending money can help you win games, but doesn’t guarantee anything.
The Mets spent big and missed the playoffs, while Cleveland and Tampa Bay didn’t spend much and made it to the postseason and world series.
Having money gives teams more opportunities to build a talented team, but the games still have to be played.
Overall baseball isn’t about who’s pocket is the deepest
